content: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) can serve as a temporary measure to reverse or slow the progression of respiratory failure in individuals with cystic fibrosis by providing ventilatory support without the need for tracheal intubation. By enhancing airflow and gas exchange while reducing the effort required for breathing, NIV improves lung mechanics and functions as an external respiratory muscle. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of NIV versus no NIV in individuals with cystic fibrosis, specifically for airway clearance, during sleep, and during exercise. The search for relevant studies included comprehensive electronic database searches, handsearching of journals, and conference proceedings, with the most recent search conducted on August 8, 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they compared pressure-preset or volume-preset NIV to no NIV in individuals with acute or chronic respiratory failure due to cystic fibrosis. A total of 10 trials involving 191 participants met the inclusion criteria. Seven trials assessed single treatment sessions, while one trial each evaluated interventions lasting two weeks, six weeks, and three months. Blinding was only feasible for outcome assessors in trials involving airway clearance and overnight ventilatory support. Most trials had an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient descriptions of blinding procedures, although the six-week trial was judged to have a low risk of bias across all domains. One single-session trial had a low risk of bias for randomization, while the remaining trials had unclear risks. Most trials demonstrated a low risk of bias for incomplete outcome data and selective reporting. Six trials (151 participants) investigated the use of NIV for airway clearance compared to alternative chest physiotherapy methods, such as active cycle of breathing techniques or positive expiratory pressure. Interfaces used included nasal masks (three trials), nasal masks or mouthpieces (one trial), and face masks (one trial), while one trial did not specify the interface. Three trials reported on quality of life, a primary outcome of the review. Secondary outcomes suggested that airway clearance might be easier with NIV, and individuals with cystic fibrosis may prefer it. However, there was no evidence that NIV increased sputum expectoration, although some lung function parameters improved. Three trials (27 participants) evaluated NIV for overnight ventilatory support compared to oxygen or room air. Two trials used nasal masks, while one used either nasal or full-face masks. These trials reported on quality of life and symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing, which were primary outcomes. Secondary outcomes included lung function, gas exchange, treatment adherence, patient preference, and nocturnal transcutaneous carbon dioxide levels. Due to the small sample sizes and statistical inconsistencies, results varied between the RevMan analyses and the original trial data. No significant differences were observed between NIV and oxygen or room air, except for exercise performance, which improved significantly with NIV compared to room air over six weeks. One trial (13 participants) assessed the impact of NIV on exercise capacity, but the interface used was unclear. This trial did not report on any primary outcomes and found no significant differences between NIV and no NIV for any outcomes. Adverse effects were reported in three trials. In one trial evaluating NIV for airway clearance, a participant withdrew due to pain during respiratory muscle testing. In a trial assessing overnight NIV, one participant could not tolerate an increase in inspiratory positive airway pressure, while another trial in the same setting reported that one participant could not tolerate the NIV mask, one developed a pneumothorax while breathing room air, and two experienced aerophagia, which resolved after reducing inspiratory positive airway pressure. In conclusion, NIV may be a valuable adjunct to other airway clearance techniques, particularly for individuals with cystic fibrosis who struggle to expectorate sputum. When used alongside oxygen therapy, NIV may improve gas exchange during sleep more effectively than oxygen alone in moderate to severe disease. However, the effects of NIV on exercise remain unclear. Most evidence supporting the benefits of NIV comes from single treatment sessions with small participant numbers. The impact of NIV on pulmonary exacerbations and long-term disease progression is still uncertain. There is a pressing need for adequately powered, long-term RCTs to evaluate the clinical effects of NIV on airway clearance and exercise in cystic fibrosis.
